📖 About the Simulation
Physics:
A spin-½ in a constant magnetic field \(B\hat{z}\) picks up opposite phases on \(|\uparrow\rangle\) and \(|\downarrow\rangle\), producing Larmor precession of the Bloch vector about the z-axis at rate \(\mu B\). Measuring \(\hat S^x\) gives outcomes \(\pm \hbar/2\) with time-dependent probabilities, while the \(\hat S^z\) probabilities stay fixed. The display uses \(\hbar=1\).
Conventions:
The state is restricted to \(\alpha|\uparrow\rangle+\beta|\downarrow\rangle\) with \(\alpha\) real and \(\beta=\sqrt{1-\alpha^2}\), so \(|\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2=1\). Sign convention: \(H=-\omega_{0}\hat S_{z}\), \(\omega_{0}=\mu B\), and \(\hbar=1\).
Visuals:
Top: Bloch sphere showing the Bloch vector \(n=\langle\sigma\rangle\) and its circular precession path (drag to rotate). Bottom: \(P_+\) for an \(\hat S^x\) measurement. The probability axis is fixed to \([0,1]\).
Controls:
\(\alpha\) sets the \(|\uparrow\rangle\) amplitude, \(\beta=\sqrt{1-\alpha^2}\), and \(\mu B\) sets the precession rate. Speed scales the animation clock. Use Reset/Pause to control playback.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Spin in a magnetic field

Here’s our setup. A spin-½ sits in a uniform magnetic field along z. Its state is α|↑⟩ + β|↓⟩, with β = √(1 − α²), and you can see it drawn as the arrow on the Bloch sphere. Our question, at every instant, is P+ — the probability that a measurement of Sx returns +ℏ/2.

2 · Prepared along z

Let’s start at the pole. Set α = 1, so the spin is prepared exactly along +z. What do you think P+ does as time runs?

3 · Prepared along x

Now let’s tip it right over. With α = β = 1/√2, the arrow starts along +x. Over a long run, what range do you think P+ covers?

4 · A small tilt

So what about somewhere in between? Set α = 0.98, a spin tilted only slightly from +z. Over a long run, what range do you expect P+ to cover?

5 · A stronger field

One last experiment. Keep this state and double μB from 1.0 to 2.0. How long do you think one full cycle of P+ takes now?

The Physics

Spin precession and the Sˣ measurement probability · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A spin-½ sits in a magnetic field along z, and the sim asks, at every instant, how likely a measurement of Sx is to return +ħ/2. The same picture, a spin that precesses and is read out along a different axis, underlies magnetic resonance.

What you'll learn

  • What a measurement of Sx can return, and what P+ is the probability of.
  • How P+ is tied to the arrow on the Bloch sphere.
  • How the size of the P+ oscillation depends on α, and how its rate depends on μB.
  • Which quantities change in time and which stay fixed.
The state is an arrow on the sphere. The field turns it about z; Sx is measured along x.

What's on screen

  • Bloch sphere (top): the state as a blue arrow with a fading trail, and the blue circle it follows. Axes: x pink, y amber, z light blue.
  • |→⟩, |←⟩ (pink) on the ±x ends, |↑⟩, |↓⟩ (blue) on the poles.
  • P+(t) (bottom): the blue curve over two periods, with a cursor at the current time.
  • Output and state panels: the clock t, the current P+, the starting state |ψ(0)⟩ and the P+ equation.
See itRun the opening settings. Watch for: the blue arrow turning about the vertical z axis while P+ in the card keeps changing.

03

What an Sx measurement can return

A measurement of Sx returns one of two values, +ħ/2 or −ħ/2. P+ is the probability of +ħ/2. It lies between 0 and 1 and is not a component of the spin. In the sim the field is along z:

The sim's Hamiltonian and sign convention.

The two Sx outcomes belong to the states |→⟩ and |←⟩, which the sim labels on the sphere. In the z basis:

The x basis.

P+ is the weight of |→⟩ in the state. A spin prepared exactly along z, |↑⟩, is an equal superposition of |→⟩ and |←⟩, so for it both outcomes have probability ½.

Key idea. P+ = |⟨→|ψ⟩|², the probability of one outcome. It is not the x-component of the spin.
See itPrepare the spin along +z (α = 1). Watch for: the arrow sitting on the north pole while P+ stays at one value.
04

How the field moves the odds

The field gives the two z-amplitudes opposite phases. Only their relative phase, μBt, matters for P+.

The starting state and its evolution.

Projecting onto |→⟩ gives the curve on screen:

The sim's P+ equation.
  • The ½ is the average value. The cosine is the interference between the |↑⟩ and |↓⟩ amplitudes.
  • On the sphere, the arrow turns about z at the Larmor rate μB, and P+ = ½(1 + nx), where nx is the arrow's x-coordinate.
See itStart on the equator, with the arrow along +x (α = β). Watch for: P+ reading 1 when the arrow points at |→⟩ and 0 when it points at |←⟩.
05

What sets the swing

P+ runs between ½ − αβ and ½ + αβ. Its swing is 2αβ, which equals sin θ, where θ is the angle of the arrow from +z.

The tilt on the left fixes the swing on the right (μB = 1).
  • The swing is largest, a full 0 to 1, for α = β = 1/√2, with the arrow on the equator.
  • It is zero for α = 1 or β = 1, with the arrow on a pole.
  • It depends on the product αβ, so α = 0.6 and α = 0.8 give the same swing.
α μB

These sliders move the sim too. β follows α.

See itRun one cycle each at α = 1, 0.90 and 0.71. Watch for: the card listing the lowest and highest P+ of each run.
06

What sets the rate

The arrow makes one turn about z in the time T = 2π/μB, and P+ repeats with the same period. Doubling μB halves T.

  • The time axis of the plot is ruled in units of π/μB and always spans 4π/μB, two periods. Changing μB therefore does not change the drawn curve; only the numbers on the t readout change.
  • The two sliders do different jobs: α sets how far P+ swings, and μB sets how fast it does so.
See itTime how long P+ takes to fall from 1 to ½ at μB = 1, then at μB = 2. Watch for: the card showing the two times side by side.
07

What stays fixed, and what is measured

The Bloch vector the sim draws, and the quantities that do not move.
  • P+ + P− = 1: these are the only two outcomes.
  • The z odds never change. The field only turns the arrow about z, so its height nz = α² − β² and the probability α² of +ħ/2 along z stay constant.
  • ⟨Sx⟩ = (ħ/2)(P+ − P−) is the average of the two outcomes. It lies between −ħ/2 and +ħ/2.
  • |↑⟩ and |↓⟩ are the energy eigenstates here. A spin prepared in one of them only gains an overall phase, so its arrow never moves.
  • Nothing is measured on screen. The sim evolves one state, with no collapse and no randomness, and plots the probability a measurement would have.
See itUse α = 0.8 and watch the arrow while P+ changes. Watch for: the arrow circling at a constant height above the equator while P+ rises and falls.
08

Where it matters

  • The sim's μB is the Larmor frequency ω₀ = γB. Change the particle and only γ changes; the rest of this sheet carries over.
  • MRI. A proton in a 1.5 T scanner precesses at about 63.9 MHz, the radio frequency the scanner transmits and listens at.
  • Electron spin resonance. An electron's γ is about 658 times a proton's: at 0.35 T it precesses at about 9.81 GHz, in the microwave band.
  • Ramsey-type measurements. A spin prepared on the equator is left to precess for a time t and then read out along x. The signal is the curve of this sim with α = β.
Go deeper: the sign of the field
  • With H = −μB Sz the Bloch vector is n = (2αβ cos μBt, −2αβ sin μBt, α² − β²): it turns from +x towards −y.
  • The opposite sign turns it the other way. P+ depends only on cos μBt, so it does not change.
09

Summary

In one line. A spin-½ in a field along z precesses at ω₀ = μB, and the probability that Sx returns +ħ/2 is P+ = ½(1 + 2αβ cos μBt).

Key points

  • Sx returns only ±ħ/2. P+ is the probability of +ħ/2.
  • P+ = ½(1 + nx): it follows the arrow's x-coordinate.
  • The swing 2αβ is set by the preparation; the period 2π/μB by the field.
  • The z odds are constant, and nothing is measured on screen.

Common mix-ups

  • "The spin points along z, so P+ = 0." Sx never returns 0. |↑⟩ is an equal superposition of |→⟩ and |←⟩, so P+ = ½.
  • "P+ is the x-component of the spin." The component is ⟨Sx⟩ = (ħ/2)(P+ − P−). On a pole P+ = ½ while ⟨Sx⟩ = 0.
  • "A stronger field makes P+ swing wider." μB changes only the rate. The swing is 2αβ.

Things to try on your own

  • Set α = 0.6, then α = 0.8, and compare the P+ range in each case.
  • Set μB = 4 and use the t readout to find the time of the first minimum of P+. Compare it with π/μB.
  • Drag the sphere to look down on it from above and follow the arrow's tip around its circle.
